In [[algebraic geometry]], '''Bloch's higher Chow groups''', a generalization of [[Chow group]], is a precursor and a basic example of [[motivic cohomology]] (for smooth varieties). It was introduced by [[Spencer Bloch]] {{harv|Bloch|1986}} and the basic theory has been developed by Bloch and [[Marc Levine (mathematician)|Marc Levine]].

In more precise terms, a theorem of Voevodsky<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.claymath.org/library/monographs/cmim02.pdf|title=Lecture Notes on Motivic Cohomology|publisher=Clay Math Monographs|pages=159}}</ref> implies: for a [[smooth scheme]] ''X'' over a field and integers ''p'', ''q'', there is a natural isomorphism
:<math>\operatorname{H}^p(X; \mathbb{Z}(q)) \simeq \operatorname{CH}^q(X, 2q - p)</math>
between motivic cohomology groups and higher Chow groups.

== Motivation ==
One of the motivations for higher Chow groups comes from homotopy theory. In particular, if <math>\alpha,\beta \in Z_*(X)</math> are algebraic cycles in <math>X</math> which are rationally equivalent via a cycle <math>\gamma \in Z_*(X\times \Delta^1)</math>, then <math>\gamma</math> can be thought of as a path between <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>, and the higher Chow groups are meant to encode the information of higher homotopy coherence. For example,<blockquote><math>\text{CH}^*(X,0)</math></blockquote>can be thought of as the homotopy classes of cycles while<blockquote><math>\text{CH}^*(X,1)</math></blockquote>can be thought of as the homotopy classes of homotopies of cycles.

== Definition ==
Let ''X'' be a quasi-projective algebraic scheme over a field (“algebraic” means separated and of finite type).

For each integer <math>q \ge 0</math>, define
:<math>\Delta^q = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}[t_0, \dots, t_q]/(t_0 + \dots + t_q - 1)),</math>
which is an algebraic analog of a standard ''q''-simplex. For each sequence <math>0 \le i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_r \le q</math>, the closed subscheme <math>t_{i_1} = t_{i_2} = \cdots = t_{i_r} = 0</math>, which is isomorphic to <math>\Delta^{q-r}</math>, is called a face of <math>\Delta^q</math>.

For each ''i'', there is the embedding
:<math>\partial_{q, i}: \Delta^{q-1} \overset{\sim}\to \{ t_i = 0 \} \subset \Delta^q.</math>

We write <math>Z_i(X)</math> for the group of [[algebraic cycle|algebraic ''i''-cycles]] on ''X'' and  <math>z_r(X, q) \subset Z_{r+q}(X \times \Delta^q)</math> for the subgroup generated by closed subvarieties that [[proper intersection|intersect properly]] with <math>X \times F</math> for each face ''F'' of <math>\Delta^q</math>.

Since <math>\partial_{X, q, i} = \operatorname{id}_X \times \partial_{q, i}: X \times \Delta^{q-1} \hookrightarrow X \times \Delta^q</math> is an effective Cartier divisor, there is the [[Gysin homomorphism]]:
:<math>\partial_{X, q, i}^*: z_r(X, q) \to z_r(X, q-1)</math>,
that (by definition) maps a subvariety ''V'' to the [[scheme-theoretic intersection|intersection]] <math>(X \times \{ t_i = 0 \}) \cap V.</math>

Define the boundary operator <math>d_q = \sum_{i=0}^q (-1)^i \partial_{X, q, i}^*</math> which yields the [[chain complex]]
:<math>\cdots \to z_r(X, q) \overset{d_q}\to z_r(X, q-1) \overset{d_{q-1}}\to \cdots \overset{d_1}\to z_r(X, 0).</math>

Finally, the ''q''-th higher Chow group of ''X'' is defined as the ''q''-th homology of the above complex:
:<math>\operatorname{CH}_r(X, q) := \operatorname{H}_q(z_r(X, \cdot)).</math>

(More simply, since <math>z_r(X, \cdot)</math> is naturally a simplicial [[abelian group]], in view of the [[Dold–Kan correspondence]], higher Chow groups can also be defined as homotopy groups <math>\operatorname{CH}_r(X, q) := \pi_q z_r(X, \cdot)</math>.)

For example, if <math>V \subset X \times \Delta^1</math><ref>Here, we identify <math>\Delta^1</math> with a subscheme of <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> and then, without loss of generality, assume one vertex is the origin 0 and the other is ∞.</ref> is a closed subvariety such that the intersections <math>V(0), V(\infty)</math> with the faces <math>0, \infty</math> are proper, then
<math>d_1(V) = V(0) - V(\infty)</math> and this means, by Proposition 1.6. in Fulton’s [[intersection theory]], that the image of <math>d_1</math> is precisely the group of cycles rationally equivalent to zero; that is,
:<math>\operatorname{CH}_r(X, 0) = </math> the ''r''-th [[Chow group]] of ''X''.

== Properties ==

=== Functoriality ===
Proper maps <math>f:X\to Y</math> are covariant between the higher chow groups while flat maps are contravariant. Also, whenever <math>Y</math> is smooth, any map to <math>Y</math> is contravariant.

=== Homotopy invariance ===
If <math>E \to X</math> is an algebraic vector bundle, then there is the homotopy equivalence<blockquote><math>\text{CH}^*(X,n) \cong \text{CH}^*(E,n)</math></blockquote>

=== Localization ===
Given a closed equidimensional subscheme <math>Y \subset X</math> there is a localization long exact sequence<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\cdots \\
\text{CH}^{*-d}(Y,2) \to \text{CH}^{*}(X,2) \to \text{CH}^{*}(U,2) \to & \\
\text{CH}^{*-d}(Y,1) \to \text{CH}^{*}(X,1) \to \text{CH}^{*}(U,1) \to & \\
\text{CH}^{*-d}(Y,0) \to \text{CH}^{*}(X,0) \to \text{CH}^{*}(U,0) \to & \text{ }0
\end{align}</math></blockquote>where <math>U = X-Y</math>. In particular, this shows the higher chow groups naturally extend the [[exact sequence]] of chow groups.

== Localization theorem ==
{{harv|Bloch|1994}} showed that, given an open subset <math>U \subset X</math>, for <math>Y = X - U</math>,
:<math>z(X, \cdot)/z(Y, \cdot) \to z(U, \cdot)</math>
is a homotopy equivalence. In particular, if <math>Y</math> has pure [[codimension]], then it yields the long exact sequence for higher Chow groups (called the localization sequence).

== Rational coefficients ==
With rational coefficients, higher Chow groups identify with a piece of [[Algebraic K-theory|algebraic <math>K</math>-theory]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Levine |first=Marc |date=1992 |title=Bloch's higher Chow groups revisited |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/?id=AST_1994__226__235_0 |journal=[[Astérisque]] |issue=226 |pages=235-320 |via=Numdam}}</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{H}^p(X; \mathbb{Q}(q)) \simeq \operatorname{CH}^q(X, 2q - p)\otimes\mathbb Q \simeq K_{2p-q}(X)^{(q)},</math>
namely the eigenspace of the [[Adams operation]] <math>\Psi^l</math> associated to the eigenvalue <math>l^q</math> (which does not depend on choice of <math>l</math>).
